title: TB9-00875
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The principal claimant, XXXX XXXX, his spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their minor children, XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX, along with the principal claimant's parents, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, seek refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and section 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
The claims were heard jointly. XXXX XXXX was appointed the designated representatives for the minor children and acted in that capacity at the hearing.
The claimants, who lived in Saudi Arabia as temporary residents, are stateless Palestinians, with the exception of XXXX XXXX XXXX.

The principal and his father were employed in Saudi Arabia. The residency permits of the principal claimant's wife and children were tied to his, while his mother's residency permit was tied to his father's residency permit. The principal claimant and his father both allege that they lost their jobs in 2018. Unable to find a new employment sponsor due to labor law policies requiring companies give preference to Saudi nationals, they decided to leave the country.

On XXXX XXXX, 2018, the principal claimant travelled to the United States with his wife and children, followed by his parents on XXXX XXXX, 2019. On XXXX XXXX, 2019, the principal claimant, his wife and children, entered Canada and filed refugee claims. On XXXX XXXX, 2019, the principal claimant's parents likewise entered Canada and filed refugee claims.

The panel determines that the claimants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, are Convention refugees pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA, but finds that XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are not Convention refugees, pursuant to section 96, and are not persons in need of protection pursuant to section 97, of the IRPA.

The determinative issues are identity, credibility, and country of reference/countries of former habitual residence. State protection and Internal Flight Alternative were also considered for the claims of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
In conducting the hearing and reaching my decision, the panel considered and applied the Chairperson's Guidelines on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.2 Identity

The principal claimant, his wife, and their daughters were born in Saudi Arabia; however, their son, XXXX XXXX XXXX, was born in the United States. The principal claimant, his wife, and their daughters hold travel documents issued by the Palestinian Authority, while their son has a passport that was issued by the government of the United States. The principal claimant likewise has a travel document issued by the Egyptian government.

The principal claimant's parents, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, were born in Gaza, Palestine. His father left Gaza with his family in or about 1967, while his mother family left Gaza with her family in or about 1968. They hold travel documents for stateless Palestinians issued by Egypt, Jordan and the Palestinian Authority.
The panel is satisfied that the claimants are stateless Palestinians, with the exception of XXXX XXXX XXXX who was born in the United States, and is a citizen of that country. Credibility

When a claimant gives evidence under oath, the testimony is presumed to be truthful unless there are valid reasons to doubt its veracity. The adult claimants testified at the hearing. The panel found that XXXX XXXX and his spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX, were not credible witnesses. Significant portions of their testimonies were based on exaggerations and embellishments designed to bolster their claims, concerning the persecution they allegedly face as stateless Palestinians in Saudi Arabia and why they cannot return to that country. The panel likewise assessed the claimants' credibility with regard to evidence concerning what constitutes countries of former habitual residence, and found XXXX XXXX XXXX was not a credible witness. Country of Former Habitual Residence (CFHR)

Given that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX were born in Gaza, and lived there for a substantial period of time before relocating to Saudi Arabia, where they resided for decades and raised their families, the panel finds that both Saudi Arabia and Palestine (Gaza) are countries of former habitual residence for XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Based on the evidence before the panel, neither Egypt nor Jordan are countries of former habitual residence for these claimants.

Although the principal claimant and his children hold travel documents issued by the Palestinian Authority, he testified that neither him nor his children have been to Palestine. The panel therefore finds it is not a country of former habitual residence for him and his children.

The principal claimant testified he lived in Egypt for two years while completing his studies. The panel finds that Egypt is not a country of former habitual residence for this claimant given that his stay there was temporary in nature with no expectation of permanence.
The panel finds that Saudi Arabia is the sole country of former habitual residence for XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX.

The principal claimant's wife was born in Saudi Arabia. In her Basis of Claim (BOC) form she was asked "When did you leave your country," to which responded "I was in Gaza for a short visit with my family in 2000."3 At the hearing, XXXX XXXX XXXX's story evolved. She testified that she visited Palestine (Gaza) before the year 2000, and travelled there a total of five (5) times with her parents. XXXX XXXX XXXX testified they went for vacation as a family and to visit cousins, who have since passed. She stated she only has a maternal uncle in Gaza currently.

When asked how long she spent in Palestine during these visits, XXXX XXXX XXXX stated she did not remember how long she stayed there on the first visit, however on the other four occasions she stayed there approximately five to six months on each occasion. When asked what she did there, she stated that her late father would visit relatives and that her father had a house there which was later destroyed. XXXX XXXX XXXX testified that most of the trips happened before she was six years old, but the last trip happened in the year 2000 when she was nine. XXXX XXXX XXXX later told the panel that she did not recall how long they stayed in Gaza during the times that she travelled there before she was six years old. She also did not have the travel documents she used to travel to Gaza. When asked how she recalls she was there for 5 to 6 months she stated it was vacation that her family took annually. Explaining her father's lengthy absence from his job in Saudi Arabia, she stated he worked for a XXXX, not a XXXX XXXX. While possible, the panel finds it unlikely that the principal claimant's father, a foreign worker in Saudi Arabia, would be allowed to leave his employment for five to six months annually.

The panel asked XXXX XXXX XXXX why she stated at question 2 (e) of BOC form she was only in Gaza for a short visit in 2000, and not stated she stayed 5 to 6 months. In response she stated when she completed the BOC form she did not remember and she asked her mother who told her it was a short visit. The panel asked her how is it that she remembered on the day of the hearing that she had visited Gaza for 5-6 months. XXXX XXXX XXXX stated she only recalled when she spoke to her mother two days before the hearing about the time spent in Gaza. She stated the conversation arose because when she met with her counsel to prepare for the hearing she was told that she needed to have information about the time that she spent in Gaza. [21] The panel notes that although she testified to this effect at the hearing, XXXX XXXX XXXX likewise did not indicate in her BOC form that she had visited Gaza before the year 2000, stating only that she went there for a short visit in 2000. The panel asked why she did not mention the visits to Gaza before 2000. She stated "no specific reason." The panel rejects this explanation. The country of former habitual residence is an essential issue in this claim given that most of the claimants are stateless. The claimants are represented by experienced counsel, who assisted them in completing the BOC forms. In her BOC form, XXXX XXXX XXXX wrote that she went to Gaza for a short visit in 2000. In the panel's view, XXXX XXXX XXXX would have indicated in the BOC form that she visited Gaza on more than one occasion if this was true. [22] Given the foregoing, the panel does not find XXXX XXXX XXXX's testimony regarding her visits to Gaza, before the year 2000, and the length of time she stayed there, credible. [23] Following the refugee hearing, the claimants disclosed several post-hearing documents,4 including a Control Exit Card for XXXX XXXX XXXX and her family pertaining to the visit to Gaza in 2000, along with a United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) Registration Card naming all the family members, and a letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX's mother confirming the family went to Gaza in 2000, remaining there for approximately four (4) months.5 In regard to whether Palestine is a CFHR for XXXX XXXX XXXX, the UNRWA Registration Card has low probative value and the panel gives it little weight. The UNRWA Registration Card is verification she is a stateless Palestinian. It was issued in 1994, about four (4) years after XXXX XXXX XXXX's birth. Although it lists, as the "RESIDENTIAL CENTRE," the village where her family is from, she was living in Saudi Arabia at the time with her family, not Palestine. [24] The information in the mother's letter is consistent with XXXX XXXX XXXX's BOC form, indicating she went to Gaza in 2000 and consistent with the details found in the Control Exit Card, showing they left Gaza on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX2000, as her mother alleges. XXXX XXXX XXXX's mother wrote that the family left Saudi Arabia on XXXX XXXX XXXX/2000 to visit relatives in Gaza and left on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX2000, explaining that although her husband generally had forty (40) days annual vacation, he had not taken vacation in the three previous years and was entitled to 120 days of vacation in 2000.6 The family stayed a little over the 120 days because XXXX XXXX XXXX's aunt was ill. The information in this letter is different from XXXX XXXX XXXX's testimony where she alleged that she visited Gaza on five (5) different occasions with her family, and that on at least four (4) of those occasions, aside from the first trip, they stayed in Gaza for 5 to 6 months on each occasion for vacation. The mother's letter indicates that her husband generally had forty (40) days vacation annually - not 5 to 6 months - but had 120 days total in 2000, because he had not taken vacation in the 3 preceding years. Further, XXXX XXXX XXXX's mother confirms only the one trip to Gaza in 2000, and not the four (4) others that XXXX XXXX XXXX testified about. [25] The panel finds the letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX's mother credible, given its consistency with the supporting documents. The panel gives it significant weight. However, the panel finds the information in this letter diminishes XXXX XXXX XXXX's credibility, specifically her contention that she visited Gaza on five (5) different occasions with her family, and that on at least four (4) of those occasions, aside from the first trip, they stayed in Gaza for 5 to 6 months on each occasion. The panel draws a negative credibility inference and finds on a balance of probabilities that XXXX XXXX XXXX only visited Gaza on one occasion, in the year 2000. [26] The evidence does not reveal that Palestine (Gaza) is a CFHR for XXXX XXXX XXXX. Counsel referred to a former decision of the panel, urging the panel to follow the reasoning in that decision. The panel finds that decision is distinguishable based on the facts of that case. [27] The panel acknowledges that it should not be unduly restrictive when assessing whether a country is a CFHR. However, whether a CFHR for a stateless person is a question of fact. [28] In Maarouf,7 the Federal Court held that "[t]he claimant must have established a significant period of de facto residence in the country in question." Generally, a claimant must have been admitted to a given country, with the intention of settling there for a certain period.8 The term "habitual residence" presupposes the existence of a relationship with the State that is comparable to that which exists between a citizen and his country of nationality, wherein a stateless person was admitted into a given country with a view of establishing continuous residence there for a certain time, without requiring a minimum period of residence. [29] XXXX XXXX XXXX was not admitted to Gaza with a view of establishing continuous residence there for a certain time. She was born and raised in Saudi Arabia, by parents who were born in Palestine, and testified that she went to Gaza on vacation with her parents while they were living in Saudi Arabia. Her mother also confirmed in her letter that they went to Gaza for vacation and to visit relatives on one occasion in the year 2000. There was no intention of settling in Gaza. XXXX XXXX XXXX attended both XXXX and XXXX XXXX in Saudi Arabia, later met her husband in Saudi Arabia, and lived there with her family before coming to Canada. [30] The panel finds XXXX XXXX XXXX has not established a significant period of de facto residence in Gaza. Her four months visit to Gaza for vacation does not make it a CFHR, notwithstanding the fact she holds a travel document issued by the Palestinian Authority and has an uncle in Gaza. In Qassim,9 the Court held that Iraq, where a claimant had significant family ties was not a CFHR. The claimant in Qassim was born and raised in UAE, and lived in UAE his entire life apart from two years studying in Canada and two visits with his family to Iraq. Although the claimant possessed an Iraqi identity card and two expired travel documents issued by the government of Iraq, the claimant's father was born in Iraq, and he had two aunts still residing in Iraq, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found Iraq was not a CFHR. The Court agreed, finding that the RPD did not err in identifying UAE as the sole CFHR for this claimant.10 The court rejected the applicant's argument that family ties are more important than the period of residence or duration or residence, finding it is not supported by the jurisprudence.11 [31] Based on the foregoing, the panel finds that Palestine (Gaza) is not a CFHR for XXXX XXXX XXXX. Rather, Saudi Arabia is the only CFHR for this claimant. As stated in these reasons, she was born and raised in Saudi Arabia, and spent most of her life in Saudi Arabia, until recently. As such, her fear of persecution has been assessed in relation to Saudi Arabia. Claim against the United States - XXXX XXXX XXXX [32] Upon entry to Canada, a claim was filed on behalf of XXXX XXXX XXXX, who is a citizen of the United States. At the hearing the panel was informed that no evidence would be advanced in regard to this claim. Given that no evidence was advanced with respect to his claim and there was no persuasive evidence before the panel demonstrating that he faces harm in the Unites States, the panel finds that XXXX XXXX XXXX faces no serious possibility of persecution for any Convention ground pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA and would not be subjected to any risk under section 97 of the IRPA if he were to return to the United States. Claims against Gaza [33] The claimants XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, who were born in Gaza, testified they have no right of return to Gaza which effectively amounts to persecution. XXXX XXXX likewise wrote in his narrative "that we as Palestinians are forever barred from return to the national home of the Palestinian people is itself persecutory."12 [34] The panel has not assessed the claims of XXXX XXXX, his wife, and children in relation to Palestine (Gaza), given that it is not their country of former habitual residence. [35] The panel will now examine the issue of denial of a right to return in relation to XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The denial of a right to return is not on its own sufficient to meet the Convention definition. Rather, the reasons for the denial must show persecutory intent or conduct related to a Convention ground. To understand this, the panel must examine the historical background or events which led these claimants to leave Gaza, their former habitual residence, with their parents in 1967 and 1968 respectively. [36] In 1947, a plan to partition Palestine into a Jewish and an Arab state failed, and in 1948, Israel was declared an independent state.13 When Israel won its independence, roughly 700,000 Palestinians were driven out or fled from their homes, an occurrence Palestinians call the nakba ("catastrophe").14 Many of these Palestinians ended up in neighboring states (Egypt, Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan) or in Gulf states such as Kuwait.15 In 1967, following what is known as the "Six-Day War," Israel seized East Jerusalem, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip, gaining control over the entire area that constituted Palestine under the British Mandate.16 The state of Israel thereafter began settling thousands of Jewish civilians in West Bank and Gaza.17 This period marking Israeli rule and settlement of the West Bank and Gaza again saw hundreds of thousands of Palestinians fleeing Palestine to various Arab states.18 While some left voluntarily, many were expelled from the West Bank and Gaza, to allow for Jewish settlements. [37] The claimants XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX fled with their parents and siblings during this period. XXXX and his family left Gaza around the time of the war in 1967, while XXXX's family left in 1968. [38] The United Nations UN General Assembly Resolution 194 recognizes the "right of return" for Palestinian refugees who fled after 1948. However, the "right of return" for all diaspora Palestinians is disputed by the state of Israel. Although Hamas is currently the de facto government in Gaza and the Palestinian Authority has civil and security control, in coordination with Israel in some areas of the West Bank, according to the documentary evidence Israel effectively controls the Palestinian population registry in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.19 While the Palestinian Authority issues identification documents to Palestinians in these territories, they can only do so in coordination with Israel, which has cancelled or refused registration, residency, and family unification requests for more than 230,000 Palestinians since 1967, many on grounds of remaining outside the West Bank and Gaza for too long.20 In addition, item 3.7 of Exhibit 9, cited in counsel's written submissions confirms that Egyptian travel document for Palestinians "has no power to permit its holders to enter Gaza."21 It states further: Travel between Gaza and Egypt is controlled as a practical matter by both the Egyptian and the Israeli authorities, as it is the Israeli government that gives final approval to "lists" of Palestinians who wish to travel from Gaza to or through Egypt. After the 1967 war, Israel conducted a census of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Any Palestinian not counted on that census list (those not present in the occupied territories at that time), were not given an official ID and ID number by the Israeli authorities. Any Palestinian (or immediate descendant, who must separately apply for it through family unity regulations to the Israeli authorities) not possessing an ID based on this census cannot travel into or out of the Gaza Strip, including to Egypt.22 [39] The panel finds on a balance of probabilities that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX have no right of return to Palestine and that the restriction, which has consequences of a severely prejudicial nature, amounts to persecution. Further, the panel finds the denial of the right of return is directly related to the fact they are Palestinians. [40] The panel considered whether adequate state protection would be reasonably forthcoming to these claimants. However, they are not allowed to enter Gaza, and the ruling governments in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT) are complicit in the restrictions they face. The panel finds that adequate state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming to these claimants and that they have rebutted the presumption of state protection in the circumstances of this case. [41] For the same reasons the panel finds they likewise have no internal flight alternative. [42] Although Saudi Arabia is also a country of former habitual residence for these claimants the panel accepts that they cannot return to the Saudi Arabia. XXXX, who was his wife's sponsor, testified that he was terminated from his employment in XXXX 2018, and alleges that they cannot return to Saudi Arabia because he no longer has employment, and it would be impossible to find one given his age. This evidence is consistent with the objective country documentation for Saudi Arabia which indicates that residence is conditional on a valid employment contract. [43] The panel finds that they have no right to return to the Saudi Arabia. Claims against Saudi Arabia for the remaining claimants [44] XXXX XXXX and his family allege that they faced discrimination in Saudi Arabia. Although they were born in Saudi Arabia, the government does not grant citizenship to non-Saudis born in the country. They were deprived of publicly-available services, including access to free health care, public education, and other services or rights generally accorded to Saudi nationals. XXXX XXXX had to attend XXXX in Egypt after completing XXXX XXXX. [45] The information before the panel is that non-citizens in Saudi Arabia are treated differently. For instance, persons born in Saudi Arabia to non-national fathers have no path to citizenship and are treated as non-citizens. Generally, all non-citizens must secure an employment sponsor to legally remain in the country.23 Non-citizens have no access to free services, such as public education, health care and other social services.24 Nevertheless, non-citizens may pay for most services privately. For instance, non-citizens lack access to free public education,25 with some exceptions, but can attend private schools upon payment of a fee. Further, while non-citizens have no access to healthcare at public hospitals, they can pay for services at private hospitals set up to accommodate non-nationals. [46] The claimants have failed to establish that Saudi Arabia's failure to grant citizenship as a birthright has any persecutory intent or effect. Additionally, the panel finds the treatment of non-citizens in Saudi Arabia, as it pertains to access to free public services, including public education and access to care in public hospitals, is not persecution given it is unrelated to any of the grounds set out in the definition of a Convention refugee. The claimants were not singled out on account of their Palestinian identity, and the documentary evidence makes no reference to generalised persecution of Palestinians in Saudi Arabia. Moreover, the government of Saudi Arabia does not owe the same duty to non-citizens as it does to citizens of that country. [47] Further, although non-citizens apparently do not have access to free public education,26 XXXX XXXX testified that he attended public XXXX and XXXX schools in Saudi Arabia. Hence, his education was free. When asked how he received a public education if this is generally reserved for Saudi nationals he stated the situation was good for ex-patriates at the time. XXXX XXXX testified that he had to attend XXXX in Egypt. However, the panel does not find this discriminatory. The evidence reveals that non-citizens in Saudi Arabia do not have access to free public education at the university level, and must pay for post-secondary studies. The policy does not affect only Palestinians, but rather all foreigners in the country. XXXX XXXX studied for XXXX XXXX at a XXXX XXXX XXXX, Egypt, and later decided to pursue a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in Saudi Arabia, which he paid for. The fact XXXX XXXX had to attend XXXX in Egypt and pay for his XXXX XXXX XXXX studies in Saudi Arabia, and may have to pay for his children's education, does not amount to persecution as the restriction is the result of laws of general application and suggests no persecutory intent or conduct as a result of the claimants being Palestinians. [48] XXXX XXXX testified that his daughter, XXXX XXXX, attended a private school in Saudi Arabia. Previously she attended a public school for a short period, because XXXX XXXX had connections with an influential individual within XXXX XXXX, but was later moved to a private school. XXXX XXXX alleges that his daughter had to be moved to a private school because she faced "discrimination." He alleges that the staff at the school did not think she had the right to attend a public school and although she was "bright and deserve to have best marks" she was denied an award and the good marks were given to Saudi students. Further, when she asked the teacher a question she was told to ask her mother. [49] There was no persuasive evidence before the panel that the issues XXXX XXXX faced in the public school in Saudi Arabia was because she is Palestinian. XXXX XXXX indicated the teacher did not believe she should attend a public school, generally reserved for Saudi nationals. It was also alleged in the narrative that XXXX XXXX's peers, who would have been 6 years old or younger at the time, "ostracised her as a Palestinian and a foreigner." Even if this did occur, the claimants have failed to demonstrate a serious possibility of persecution under sections 96 upon return to Saudi Arabia. XXXX XXXX stated XXXX XXXX was moved to a private school and testified that XXXX XXXX did not have any problems in the private school, informing the panel "she was taken care of in the best way." [50] XXXX XXXX wrote in his narrative that he faced "regular discrimination" in employment while living in Saudi Arabia, indicating for instance that he would frequently train Saudi workers, who were then hired as his manager. XXXX XXXX further alleges that his sponsors took advantage of their power over his life: one employer allegedly forced him to work without pay and he was told if he took sick leave he would be reported to immigration so the sponsor could find a replacement. Further, the Saudi government also imposed fees to include his dependent spouse and children under his residency permit, and despite paying high fees to the government, they received no services in return. The treatment described by XXXX XXXX was due to his status as a temporary foreign worker and the vulnerability he faced as a foreigner in Saudi Arabia. The documentary evidence reveals that the situation of foreigners in Saudi Arabia is less than ideal.27 While these occurrences were undoubtedly upsetting for the XXXX XXXX, the panel finds such experiences were unrelated to any of the grounds in the Convention refugee definition. There was no persuasive evidence before the panel indicating that XXXX XXXX was treated in this manner because of his Palestinian heritage, nor does the evidence reveal deliberate or systemic targeting of Palestinians in Saudi Arabia. [51] The panel finds that XXXX XXXX exaggerated and/or embellished his experiences in Saudi Arabia. His experiences do not show that he was discriminated against. Rather, he routinely found work and received many privileges. For instance, the evidence shows that after studying for XXXX XXXX at a XXXX XXXX XXXX, Egypt, XXXX XXXX returned to Saudi Arabia, where he immediately found work. He was gainfully employed for 16 years. In 2002, he started working in a XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX "quickly rose" to the position of XXXX according to his BOC narrative.28 In 2006, XXXX XXXX switched employers and began working in the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. In 2008, he again switched employers when he found work with the XXXX XXXX XXXX. Thereafter, XXXX XXXX decided to pursue a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. In 2013, he started working as a XXXX XXXX, with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX worked with this company from 2013 until he was terminated effective XXXX XXXX, 2018. While working with this company XXXX XXXX received many opportunities to travel overseas on important work assignments for the company. For instance, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX tasked him with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, Texas. XXXX XXXX spent 6 1/2 months in the United States, from XXXX 2016 to XXXX 2017, with his wife and children, as a result of one of his work assignments. The couple's youngest child was born in the United States during that trip. XXXX XXXX was also in the United States on business trips in in XXXX 2016 and XXXX 2017. [52] XXXX XXXX likewise discussed the difficulty he allegedly faced finding employment in Saudi Arabia, indicating that after losing his job, he was unable to find a new employment sponsor to renew his residency permit. [53] The panel finds that any difficulty that XXXX XXXX or any of the other claimants experienced finding employment has nothing to do with their Palestinian ethnicity. XXXX XXXX stated whenever he applied for jobs he was told the companies were not hiring ex-patriates. The documentary evidence indicates that due to labor law reforms, informally refer to as "Saudization," requiring companies to increase private sector employment of Saudi citizens, there are less employment opportunities for non-citizens. However, as part of the labor law reforms, the government implemented measures allowing foreign workers to switch to a new employer or to companies that employed a sufficient quota of Saudi nationals.29 [54] The panel finds that the claimants face no serious possibility of persecution in Saudi Arabia in relation to employment. There was no persuasive evidence before the panel indicating that the claimants would be denied the ability to work, albeit likely not in their field. However, "persecution does not result from the ability to work in the field of one's choosing. Rather it flows from one's inability to work at all."30 In Saudi Arabia, non-citizens can be "employed as non-citizens," provided they secure a sponsor.31 This policy applies to all non-citizens, and does not single out Palestinians. While the panel acknowledges that the latest labor law policies have likely rendered it more difficult for some workers to find employment, the panel does not find the conditions imposed by the government to regulate the job market persecutory in nature. Gender-based discrimination [55] In relation to XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX, the panel considered the discrimination faced by women in Saudi Arabia. The panel acknowledges the evidence indicating that the law and tradition in Saudi Arabia discriminate on the basis of gender.32 For instance, gender discrimination excluded women from many aspects of public life.33 The guardianship system also places restrictions on women, although according to the documentary evidence, the guardianship system does not require women to have a male guardian's permission to move freely within the country.34 The evidence appears to state that many of the restrictions women traditionally faced in Saudi Arabia have eased. For instance, women increasingly participated in political life and the ban on women driving was lifted by the government in June 2018.35 The panel accepts that women still face discrimination in the workplace. For instance, rules limited the type of work women can perform, required them to wear a veil in most workplaces, and enforced gender segregation on penalty of fines.36 [56] While women in Saudi Arabia continue to face discrimination and limits on their personal freedoms, the panel finds that cumulatively the discrimination does not rise to persecution. Denial of entry not persecution [57] Under certain circumstances, a claimant being refused entry to their country of habitual residence may constitute state persecution. However, the panel finds that not to be the situation for these claimants who allege that they would be denied entry to Saudi Arabia because their residence permits have expired and/or they have been away from the country for more than the time permissible. The documentary evidence indicates that to exit and re-enter Saudi Arabia, an individual must have an "exit/re-entry visa," which is valid for six months from the date of departure.37 The panel accepts that the claimants left Saudi Arabia more than 6 months ago, but finds that any potential denial of entry is unrelated to any of the grounds in the refugee Convention. It is mandatory that non-citizens wishing to enter or remain Saudi Arabia have a sponsor who must apply for a visa authorization and a residence permit (Iqama) on their behalf.38 Generally, the residence permit of the primary holder includes residence permits for the individual's "wife and minor children."39 This is an ordinary of law of general application that applies to everyone regardless of their nationality. [58] The panel accepts that to gain entry to Saudi Arabia the claimants must find an employment sponsor to secure a residence permit on their behalf. However, the panel finds this does not amount to persecution since these conditions do not constitute a breach of a fundamental right, but rather legal restrictions imposed by Saudi Arabia, in a legitimate attempt to regulate the job market and the manner by which foreigners enter and leave the country. Treatment of undocumented migrants [59] XXXX XXXX alleges he and his family face indefinite detention in Saudi Arabia because their residency permits have expired and Saudi Arabia has nowhere to deport them to. [60] There are reports that the authorities in Saudi Arabia have arrested, detained and deported undocumented migrants from the country. For instance, in November 2017, Saudi Arabia launched a campaign to detain foreigners found in violation of existing labor, residency, or border security laws, including those without valid residency or work permits.40 On November 23, 2018, the government announced that the campaign had netted over 2.1 million arrests, including for over 1.6 million residency law violations and over 328,000 labor law violations.41 [61] The documentary evidence confirms that penalties for remaining in Saudi Arabia without valid status include "statutory penalties such as custody, fining and deporting."42 However, the documentary evidence appears to indicate there are some exceptions to these penalties in the case of Palestinians. For instance, the Arab News is cited in a 2013 article for its report that "Saudi Arabia has exempted Palestinian and Burmese nationals who are found to be in violation of the new labor laws from deportation."43 Similarly, in 2013, Saudi newspapers reported that "de facto refugees (Palestinians, Rohingyas and those coming from war-torn countries (Syria), and probably people from Gaza) would not be deported in case or administrative irregularities.44 [62] XXXX XXXX wrote in his narrative that he is similarly-situated to two of his Palestinian friends who were detained after losing their jobs/sponsors. In the case of one friend, XXXX, his employer terminated him and threatened to report him to the authorities if XXXX did not pay him money. The sponsor later reported him and XXXX was detained for approximately one year. Another friend, XXXX, was detained after he got into an argument with the Saudi officer responsible for his immigration detention and the officer made a false accusation against him. The panel finds that XXXX XXXX's situation is distinguishable on the facts - his employer neither threatened to, or reported him to the authorities and the facts do not reveal that he was involved in a dispute with any authority figure in Saudi Arabia. [63] The panel accepts that the claimants whose sole CFHR is Saudi Arabia have no legal right to return there, in the absence of a sponsor, and that the minor claimants cannot return unless their parents secure sponsorships given that the residence permit of the primary holder includes residence permits for their minor children. The onus is on XXXX XXXX and/or his spouse to secure sponsors enabling the family to return to Saudi Arabia in a legal manner. [64] The alleged fear they would be arrested and detained upon return to Saudi Arabia is not well-founded since these claimants can only return to Saudi Arabia in a legal manner. CONCLUSION [65] In light of the preceding facts and having assessed all the evidence, the panel determines that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are Convention refugees pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA. The panel accepts their claims. [66] The panel finds that XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX have failed to establish a well-founded fear of persecution, or show that they face a serious possibility of persecution for a Convention ground in Saudi Arabia, or the United States, in the case of XXXX XXXX XXXX. Further, the panel finds that the claimants have not established on a balance of probabilities that they face a danger of torture or a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, upon return to Saudi Arabia, or the United States, in the case of XXXX XXXX XXXX. The panel therefore rejects their claims pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1)(a) and (b) of the IRPA. (signed) "A. Green" A.
